title: How Population Works
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a plug for the Science Channel's Road to Punkin Chunkin, then turn to "How Population Works," an article by Ed Grabianowski. They cover why humans congregate, demographers and population studies, complete enumeration (the census) versus sampling, and the census secrecy rule. They discuss population attributes such as age, socioeconomic data, and race, then population history: Columbus-era genocide and smallpox in the Americas, growth from 10,000 BC onward, Malthusian growth, replacement rate, bulges and bottlenecks, the Plague of Justinian and Black Death, founder effect, population density (Kowloon Walled City), population control (China's one-child policy), population decline and incentive programs in Russia, Japan and Australia. The episode closes with listener mail about Toledo, Ohio and a car with ants.
topics: Columbus and Native American population decline

segments.title: Opening banter and Punkin Chunkin plug
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with a plug for the Science Channel's Road to Punkin Chunkin and Thanksgiving broadcast, then introduce the population article.

segments.title: Why humans congregate
segments.summary: Early humans lived in bands of about thirty, and groups gained safety, cooperation and trade benefits. Demographers study natural and other populations.

segments.title: Counting people: complete enumeration and the census
segments.summary: Populations are measured by complete enumeration, a full count by census enumerators taken every ten years. The census is used to apportion House seats, and census data is kept secret for seventy-two years. A Kentucky census taker's death is mentioned.

segments.title: Sampling and random samples
segments.summary: Statisticians use formulas to determine a minimum sample size and extrapolate to the full population, with a margin of error. Random sampling is required, and phone-book sampling is criticized as biased.

segments.title: Ways to define populations: age, socioeconomics, race
segments.summary: Populations can be grouped by geography, age, continent, demographic or socioeconomic status. Baby boom effects on spending and Social Security are discussed, along with how socioeconomic and racial data can reveal medical problems, with caution about race.

segments.title: Population history: Columbus, smallpox and genocide
segments.summary: Charles C. Mann's estimate that the Americas held far more people before European contact, due to smallpox. The Taino of Hispaniola were decimated after Columbus's second voyage, and genocide is noted as a cause of rapid population change.

segments.title: Population growth, Malthus, bulges and bottlenecks
segments.summary: Estimated world population growth from 10,000 BC through the 20th century and into the present, with the Malthusian exponential growth model, the replacement rate of 2.33, and population bulges and bottlenecks including the Plague of Justinian, Black Death, and genetic founder effect.

segments.title: Density, population control and decline
segments.summary: Kowloon Walled City is cited as the densest place ever. Population control such as China's one-child policy is discussed alongside the problems of population decline and incentive programs in Russia, Japan and Australia. The hosts close with a note on birth control and the article search.
